summary: A quieter day in Ottawa: the Supreme Court rules today on Quebec's religious-symbols law, and Carney heads to Yellowknife to announce a major northern project.
body: The biggest Canadian story of the day lands this morning: the Supreme Court of Canada is set to rule on Friday on Quebec's secularism law, known as Bill 21.[^1] The law bars many public-sector workers, including teachers, from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs, turbans or crosses on the job. Quebec shielded it with the notwithstanding clause, a section of the Charter of Rights that lets a legislature override some rights for five years at a time.[^1] Challengers include teachers, religious and civil-liberties groups, and the English Montreal School Board.[^1]

The stakes go beyond Quebec. The ruling could say whether courts can limit how governments use the notwithstanding clause, which Alberta and Saskatchewan have also used recently.[^1] Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says Quebec's right to make its own laws is at stake, while the National Council of Canadian Muslims says that if governments can override the Charter at will, rights become "suggestions".[^1] The decision was not public at the time of writing.

Also today, Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Yellowknife with Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson to announce what his office calls a major new initiative to "connect and transform Canada's North". No details were released in advance.[^2] Otherwise it was a quiet news day.
differences: Quebec's government says the case is about Quebec's right to decide its own laws; challengers say it is about whether governments can remove religious freedoms by overriding the Charter.[^1]

reads.title: Supreme Court to rule on Quebec's secularism law. Experts say the stakes could not be higher
